1.pericope_label: Behold, there shall stand up yet three kings in Persia; and the fourth shall be far richer than they all
debates: Whose words the opening verse is, and where it belongs
Which four kings are counted
Whether the chapter is history foretold or a pattern still awaiting fulfilment
outliers: Calvin rejects the reading that refers the opening to the help of another angel, and takes the words as an argument from the greater to the less spoken in the person of God
Ellicott questions the interpretation customary since Jerome, holding that similarity to past events is not enough to confine the prophecy to them
themes: An angel standing as a strength and fortress to a king he had set on his throne
Rivers dried up by an army whose wealth was still unexhausted
A prophecy that reads like a history written before the events
History repeating itself, so that one persecutor becomes the type of another

3.pericope_label: And a mighty king shall stand up, that shall rule with great dominion, and do according to his will
debates: Whether the mighty king is Alexander or an unnamed autocrat still to come
How the empire came to be broken so soon
What the phrase about one of his princes means
outliers: Ellicott declines every identification here, holding that no clue is given as to the nation this king rules and that some later autocrat may answer the description better
Calvin takes the conjunction in the fifth verse as adversative, so that the northern king is set against the southern, where others read the two clauses together
themes: A king whose rising and whose breaking are stated as one moment
A conqueror seized with disease amidst his own cups
Generals tearing the spoils from the body of their master
A family in which not one was left alive within fifteen years

6.pericope_label: For the king daughter of the south shall come to the king of the north to make an agreement: but she shall not retain the power of the arm
debates: Whether the marriage described answers to the one usually named
What the roots are from which the avenger springs
What the last clause about continuing means
outliers: Ellicott holds history irreconcilable with the prophecy on the received identification, objecting that the marriage touched the Jewish people no more than any other and that fifty years lie between the two verses
Ellicott reads the closing preposition as standing with rather than outliving, making the southern king an ally of the northern for some years
themes: A dowry of gold and silver brought to a frontier city
A wife recalled, a husband poisoned, a queen murdered
A branch from the same roots rising to avenge a sister
Images of gods carried home and set again in their proper temples

9.pericope_label: And the king of the south shall be moved with choler, and shall come forth and fight with him, even with the king of the north
debates: Which king comes into whose kingdom and returns
Whose sons are stirred up
Which king the pronouns of the battle verses refer to
outliers: Ellicott reads the ninth verse in the genitive, reversing the direction of the march that the other voices all take one way
Keil and Delitzsch single out one interpreter who refers the sons to the southern king and hold his reading shattered by the verse that follows
themes: A conqueror recalled home by a sedition behind him
A brother poisoned by his own generals for want of pay to his troops
A title meaning lover of his father, given as a mark of disgrace
A victory not followed up, and a kingdom no stronger for it

13.pericope_label: Also the robbers of thy people shall exalt themselves to establish the vision; but they shall fall
debates: Who the robbers of the people are and what vision they establish
Whether the northern king ruined the land or favoured it
Why nothing is said of the sufferings of the people in this period
outliers: Ellicott presses it as an argument against the received reading that the persecutions of this very period go unmentioned, though the prophecy is supposed to have been written for the comfort of those who suffered them
Clarke and Wesley read the closing clause as favour rather than destruction, where Ellicott renders it literally as destruction being in his hand
themes: A child of five on a throne, and two kings dividing his kingdom on paper
A senate eager to be involved in all the business of the world
Factious men who broke the one thing that could have kept a small people standing
A land excellent by no natural advantage but by the choice of God

17.pericope_label: And he shall give him the daughter of women, corrupting her: but she shall not stand on his side, neither be for him
debates: What the upright ones are that come with the king
Who the prince is that turns the reproach back
What the raiser of taxes is
outliers: Ellicott concludes the first part of the chapter by arguing that its plain sense knows only two southern kings and one northern, and that the whole is eschatological rather than historical
Calvin rejects the reading which takes the upright ones for the Jews honoured by that title, holding it too forced
themes: A daughter given in marriage as a snare, who kept faith with her husband
Islands counted so by a people not skilled in navigation
A tribute of fifteen thousand talents paid by instalments over twelve years
A taskmaster who drives a people as cattle through the richest parts of a kingdom

21.pericope_label: And in his estate shall stand up a vile person, to whom they shall not give the honour of the kingdom
debates: What makes the man vile
How he obtained a kingdom that was not given him
Whether the description fits the persecutor usually named
outliers: Ellicott doubts that the man usually identified here took the kingdom by the craft and flattery the verse describes, though he grants that the rest of the description agrees closely
Henry explains why these troubles are foretold in such detail, namely that prophecy would cease before they came and the people would need the written word
themes: A surname meaning the Illustrious turned into a nickname meaning the Madman
A king who drank in common taverns and threw stones at those who followed him
A kingdom obtained by flattering everyone who could give it
A persecutor read as the type of a greater one still to come

22.pericope_label: And after the league made with him he shall work deceitfully: for he shall come up, and shall become strong with a small people
debates: Who the prince of the covenant is
What the scattering of prey and spoil and riches means
Why the southern king failed to stand
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott both deny that the prince of the covenant is the murdered high priest, the one on historical grounds and the other because no high priest ever bore such a title
Calvin prefers the reading that makes the scattering a robbery rather than a distribution to soldiers, where Ellicott prefers the opposite
themes: Armies overflowing a land and swept away by stronger armies still
A friendship kept until the moment it is most useful to break
Handfuls of money thrown in the street for whoever fortune sends them to
A king who could have stood, had his own ministers not been bought

26.pericope_label: And both these kings hearts shall be to do mischief, and they shall speak lies at one table; but it shall not prosper
debates: Who betrays the southern king
How many kings are meant by the two who lie at one table
What the holy covenant is that the returning king sets his heart against
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch refuse to admit a third king into the passage and call every such pairing arbitrary, citing Jerome that it cannot be demonstrated from history
Keil and Delitzsch adopt Calvin reading of the holy covenant as the institution rather than the people, and quote him by name in doing so
themes: Men who ate at a table and broke the man who set it
Two kings speaking lies to each other over one board
A king who would have stripped the whole temple and was restrained
A fleet from the west, and an embassy that ordered a king home

30.pericope_label: And arms shall stand on his part, and they shall pollute the sanctuary of strength, and shall take away the daily sacrifice
debates: Who the ships from the west belong to
Whose arms stand up to pollute the sanctuary
Why the temple is called the sanctuary of strength
outliers: Clarke takes the arms for the Romans and reads the narrative as leaving the Greek kings behind at this verse, dating the abomination centuries later; Gill, Calvin, Wesley and Ellicott all keep it with the reigning king and his apostate party
Calvin rejects the reading that makes the arms the garrison set over the city, and refers them to the forsakers of the Law instead
themes: A circle drawn in the sand round a king, who dared not step out of it
A king naturally servile abroad and beyond all bounds at home
A party at home that prostituted itself to a foreign will
A sanctuary called strong to assure the faithful that its owner had not been overcome

32.pericope_label: But the people that do know their God shall be strong, and do exploits
debates: What the phrase about doing wickedly against the covenant means
Whether those who understand are teachers or simply the pious
Who falls by the sword and flame
outliers: Clarke transfers the whole passage to a later age, reading the corrupted as those pressed to sacrifice to imperial statues and the strong as Christians under persecution

Keil and Delitzsch deny that those who understand are teachers, making their example rather than their instruction the thing that moves the multitude, against Calvin who insists on the plain transitive sense
themes: Men who began in indifference to religion and ended intolerant of it
Apostates serving as the arms of a foreign tyrant
A remnant that confirms the covenant, however small
Wise men raised up in the worst times of apostasy

34.pericope_label: And some of them of understanding shall fall, to try them, and to purge, and to make them white, even to the time of the end
debates: What the little help is and why it is called little
Who the many are that cleave with flatteries
Why those who understand are allowed to fall
outliers: Clarke transfers the little help to a Christian emperor who ended persecution, and reads the flatterers as men who took the faith because the throne had; Gill reports the same view without adopting it
Keil and Delitzsch deny that the word little is contemptuous, taking it as small only beside the full deliverance still to come
themes: A handful of men who could not restore a land but kept its worship alive
Adherents gained by a cause as soon as its prospects brighten
Metal refined by fire, and cloth made white
The flower of a church perishing while its refuse flies off

36.pericope_label: And the king shall do according to his will; and he shall exalt himself, and magnify himself above every god
debates: Whether the king described here can still be the king of the earlier verses
What the desire of women means
What god of forces the king honours instead
outliers: Wesley holds that the words principally refer to the earlier king and were primarily accomplished in him, against every other voice here, all of whom find the description no longer fits
Ellicott denies that the god honoured in place of the rejected one is a name at all, reading it as fortresses, so that the religion of this king is war itself
themes: A portrait from which the features of a known man gradually fade
A king who casts aside even the worship handed down to him
Marriage trodden under foot, whether by licence or by prohibition
War honoured as a god, and all a treasury spent upon it

38.pericope_label: But in his estate shall he honour the God of forces: and a god whom his fathers knew not shall he honour with gold, and silver
debates: Whether the god of forces is a proper name and which deity it is
How a king who despises all gods can honour one
Who is given rule over many and what land is divided
outliers: Keil and Delitzsch dismiss every proposed identification of this god by the clause that follows, since none of the candidates could be called unknown to his fathers
Calvin refers the contradiction to a people who kept the appearance of piety while holding their own gods in contempt, valuing only the one bound by title to themselves
themes: A god named from towers and fortresses
A supreme deity who was nobody at all without his local title
Shrines decked with gold, silver and precious stones
Conquered land parcelled out as the wages of assistance

40.pericope_label: And at the time of the end shall the king of the south push at him: and the king of the north shall come against him like a whirlwind
debates: Who the two kings are at the time of the end
Why three peoples escape while others fall
What is meant by the time of the end
outliers: Four different schemes are proposed for the closing war: a last campaign by the earlier king, a later pair of powers, the Romans, and an end-time conflict, and each voice rejects the others
Wesley alone explains the escape of the three peoples by their having helped the invader against the people of God, where the usual answer is that they lay off his route
themes: A portrait from which the last line of a known face has gone
A whirlwind of chariots, horsemen and many ships
Peoples who kept their deserts and were paid to let the caravans pass
A land under divine protection left open to robbery on every side

43.pericope_label: And he shall plant the tabernacles of his palace between the seas in the glorious holy mountain; yet he shall come to his end, and none shall help him
debates: What the tidings from east and north are
What the tents of his palace are
Which seas the king pitches between
outliers: Ellicott gives three reasons of geography and history why the death described cannot be that of the king usually named, and Keil and Delitzsch agree that the account contradicts the facts
Calvin reads the tents as the deliberate policy of a power that would let no place grow dignified enough to rebel, rather than as the ordinary camp of an army
themes: A conqueror to whom every fortified city lies open
News from two quarters that turns a victor back in fury
A palace-tent whose poles are driven deep, ringed by the tents of servants
A king who comes to his end with none to help him
